author: A Robot
objectives: Students will represent a two-dimensional vector by its magnitude and direction, and equivalently by its horizontal and vertical components.
Students will add two or more vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method and identify the resultant vector.
Students will decompose a vector into components along the x- and y-axes using right-triangle trigonometry, and reconstruct the original vector from its components.
Students will explain why the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of one another.
Students will describe how the horizontal velocity, vertical velocity, and position of a projectile change over the course of its flight.
Students will predict how changes in initial launch angle and launch speed affect the trajectory, range, and maximum height of a projectile.

modules.description: An introduction to vectors as mathematical objects with magnitude and direction in 3D space.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will represent a two-dimensional vector by its magnitude and direction.
Students will distinguish vectors from scalar quantities.

components.scriptDescription: Calculates the length and angle of the vector arrow and updates the text labels dynamically.

clips.changeMeaning: Initialize the vector arrow and labels in the 3D workspace
clips.narration: Welcome to the lab on vectors and projectile motion. Before us is a vector, represented by this arrow. Notice it has a clear tail at the origin, a shaft, and a head. Floating near it are two values: its magnitude, or length, and its direction, represented by angles relative to our 3D axes.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the interactive nature of the vector and difference from scalars
clips.narration: Unlike scalar quantities like temperature or mass, which only have a size, vectors have both size and direction. Grab the head of the arrow and drag it around. Watch how the magnitude and direction values update in real time as you change its orientation. You can also physically move around the arrow to view it from different perspectives.

modules.description: Demonstration of graphical vector addition using the tip-to-tail method.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will add two or more vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method.
Students will identify the resultant vector and demonstrate the commutative property of vector addition.

components.scriptDescription: Maintains its tail at the first vector's tail and its head at the second vector's head.

clips.changeMeaning: Show two vectors positioned tip-to-tail to form a resultant
clips.narration: Here we have two vectors: a blue one starting at the origin, and a green one placed starting at the tip of the blue one. This is the tip-to-tail method of vector addition. The red arrow drawn from the tail of the first to the head of the second is the resultant vector—the sum of the two.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrate that vector addition order does not matter
clips.narration: Vector addition is commutative; the order doesn't matter. If we place the green vector at the origin and add the blue vector to its tip, the red resultant vector remains exactly the same. Try grabbing the blue or green vectors to see how the resultant dynamically updates.

modules.description: Breaking a vector into its orthogonal components along the x, y, and z axes.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will decompose a vector into components along the x- and y-axes using right-triangle trigonometry.
Students will reconstruct the original vector from its components.

components.scriptDescription: Forces the main vector to equal the sum of x, y, and z components dynamically as they are resized.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the concept of breaking a vector into components
clips.narration: We can also think of vector addition in reverse. This is called vector decomposition. Here, a single vector has been broken down into three component arrows along the x, y, and z axes. Notice how they add up tip-to-tail to perfectly reconstruct the original vector.

clips.changeMeaning: Allow interaction with components to see the original vector change
clips.narration: Try grabbing and resizing any of the colored component arrows. As you lengthen or shorten a component along its axis, the original vector updates to reflect the new sum. By right-triangle trigonometry, these components relate directly to the original vector's magnitude and direction.

modules.description: Setting up the projectile motion problem as a 2D application of vectors.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will recognize that projectile motion under gravity is a genuinely two-dimensional problem.

clips.changeMeaning: Transition the workspace to a 2D physical scenario for projectiles
clips.narration: Now let's apply these vector tools to a physical problem: projectile motion. Since gravity acts only downwards and there is no horizontal force, this motion happens entirely in a vertical 2D plane. Here is a projectile with its initial velocity vector pointing up and to the right.

modules.description: Demonstration of the independence of horizontal and vertical motion during a projectile's flight.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will explain why horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent.
Students will describe how horizontal and vertical velocities change over the course of flight.

components.scriptDescription: Animates the ball along a parabolic trajectory, drawing a trail, and updating the horizontal and vertical component arrows on every frame to match current velocity.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the velocity vector broken into components during flight
clips.narration: Watch as we launch the projectile. The initial velocity is decomposed into a horizontal component and a vertical component. Notice how the horizontal component stays exactly the same length throughout the entire flight, while the vertical component shrinks as it rises, hits zero at the peak, and grows downward as it falls.

clips.changeMeaning: Switch the perspective to overhead to isolate horizontal motion
clips.narration: The horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent. If we look from directly overhead, the parabola disappears—we only see a ball moving to the right at a steady, constant speed, totally unaffected by gravity.

modules.description: An interactive exploration to find the launch angle that produces maximum range.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will predict how changes in launch angle affect range.
Students will identify that 45 degrees produces maximum range for a given speed.

components.scriptDescription: Provides an interactive AR panel to adjust angle and speed, handles the launch button event, and logs results to the history panel.

clips.changeMeaning: Provide UI for students to test launch angles and find max range
clips.narration: Now you have control. Adjust the initial launch angle and speed using the controls, and hit launch. The trajectory will trace its path, and your results will be logged in the history panel. Try to discover which launch angle produces the maximum range for a given speed.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the 45 degree maximum range result and explain complementary angles
clips.narration: As you likely discovered, for any fixed speed, a 45-degree angle maximizes the range. At 45 degrees, the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity are perfectly equal. You may also have noticed that complementary angles—like 30 and 60 degrees—land in the exact same spot!

modules.description: Applying vector decomposition and projectile concepts to a targeting challenge.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will apply knowledge of projectile motion to solve a practical targeting problem.
Students will confirm that complementary angles produce identical ranges.

components.scriptDescription: Provides an interactive AR panel to adjust angle and speed, handles the launch button event.
Detects if the projectile hits the target pad, plays a success effect, and moves the pad to a new random location.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the target pad and explain the targeting objective
clips.narration: Let's test your understanding. A target has appeared on the ground plane. Adjust your launch angle and speed to hit it. Once you hit the target, it will move to a new location.

clips.changeMeaning: Prompt the user to find both complementary angle solutions for the target
clips.narration: Remember our previous finding: for any given distance shorter than the maximum range, there are two angles that will hit the target—a high, looping path and a low, direct path. See if you can hit the same target with both angles!

modules.description: A free-exploration sandbox allowing manipulation of all projectile variables.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will freely investigate how height and gravity changes affect projectile trajectories.

components.scriptDescription: Advanced control panel that exposes sliders for Launch Angle, Initial Speed, Platform Height, and Gravity Strength. Updates environment physics dynamically.

clips.changeMeaning: Enable all sandbox variables for free and unrestricted exploration
clips.narration: You've unlocked the sandbox! You now have full control over the initial height and even the strength of gravity, along with speed and angle. What happens to the range when gravity is halved? If you launch from a 50-meter platform, is 45 degrees still the optimal angle for maximum range? Experiment and find out!

modules.description: A recap of the core concepts covered in the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will review and synthesize the six major concept areas of vectors and projectile motion.

components.text:
Lab Complete!
- Vectors: Magnitude & Direction
- Tip-to-Tail Addition
- Vector Decomposition
- Projectiles as 2D Vectors
- Independence of Motion
- 45-Degree Max Range

clips.changeMeaning: Show the final summary text of all physics concepts learned
clips.narration: Great work. In this lab, you've seen vectors as quantities with magnitude and direction. You added them graphically, decomposed them into components, and used those components to understand projectile motion. You've seen firsthand that horizontal and vertical motion are completely independent under gravity. Thank you for completing the lab.
